blocks.text: Stand holding a 25 kg bag of rice on your head for ten minutes and you will be exhausted — yet a physicist will tell you that you did no work at all. Work in physics has a precise meaning, and if the load does not move in the direction of the force, the work done on it is exactly zero.

blocks.title: Work
blocks.text: Work is done when a force moves its point of application in the direction of the force. It equals the force multiplied by the distance moved in the direction of the force, and is measured in joules (J). One joule is the work done when a force of one newton moves a body one metre along its line of action.

blocks.caption: θ is the angle between the force and the displacement; θ = 0° gives simply W = Fs

blocks.markdown:
Two consequences follow immediately from the $\cos\theta$ factor:

- If the force is **perpendicular** to the motion, $\cos 90^{\circ} = 0$, so **no work is done**. A porter walking along a level road with a load on his head does no work on the load, because the supporting force is vertical while the motion is horizontal.
- If the force **opposes** the motion, $\cos 180^{\circ} = -1$, so the work is negative. Friction always does negative work.

### Kinetic and potential energy

**Energy** is the capacity to do work, measured in joules like work itself.

**Kinetic energy** is the energy a body has because of its motion:

$$E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}$$

**Gravitational potential energy** is the energy a body has because of its height:

$$E_p = mgh$$

Note the $v^{2}$ in kinetic energy. Doubling the speed of a car **quadruples** its kinetic energy — which is why speed matters so much more than mass in a crash.

blocks.title: Work done dragging a crate
blocks.prompt: A man pulls a crate 10 m along level ground using a rope that makes an angle of 60° with the horizontal. The tension in the rope is 100 N. Calculate the work done by the man.

steps.text: Only the component of the force along the direction of motion does work.
Identify each quantity. The angle between the rope and the displacement is 60°.
Evaluate the work with its unit.
Interpret: the effective horizontal pull is only 50 N, so pulling at a shallower angle would transfer more energy to the crate for the same tension.

blocks.markdown:
### Conservation of mechanical energy

When only gravity does work — no friction, no air resistance — the sum of kinetic and potential energy stays constant:

$$E_k + E_p = \text{constant}$$

So for a falling body, $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2} = mgh$, and the mass cancels to give $v = \sqrt{2gh}$. This is the energy route to the same result the equations of motion give, and it is often much quicker.

blocks.title: A pendulum bob released from a height
blocks.prompt: A pendulum bob of mass 0.20 kg is pulled aside until it is 0.45 m above its lowest point, then released. Taking g = 10 m/s² and neglecting air resistance, find its speed as it passes through the lowest point.

steps.text: At the release point the bob is at rest, so all its energy is potential.
At the lowest point all of that has become kinetic energy, since no friction acts.
Take the square root and attach the unit.
Check with v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 10 × 0.45) = √9 = 3.0 m/s. The mass cancelled, so any bob released from that height arrives at the same speed.

Solar (light) energy → electrical energy → chemical energy
Kinetic energy → potential energy, then back again
blocks.caption: Energy transformations. Energy is never created or destroyed, only converted.

blocks.title: Watch the height, not the path
blocks.text: Gravitational potential energy depends only on the VERTICAL height gained. Pushing a crate 10 m up a gentle ramp that rises 2 m gives it mg × 2 of potential energy, not mg × 10. Any extra work you did went into overcoming friction.

blocks.title: WAEC and JAMB tip
blocks.text: When a question involves speed and height together, reach for energy conservation before the equations of motion. Setting ½mv² = mgh cancels the mass and usually gets you there in one line.

points: Work = force × distance moved in the direction of the force, W = Fs cos θ, measured in joules.
No work is done when the force is perpendicular to the displacement.
Kinetic energy is ½mv² and gravitational potential energy is mgh.
Because kinetic energy depends on v², doubling the speed quadruples the kinetic energy.
When only gravity does work, mechanical energy is conserved, giving v = √(2gh) independent of mass.
